questions.subtopic: 2A3 Vulnerability management. Severity scores in the register
questions.question: A bank's vulnerability team proposes copying each finding's CVSS Base score straight into the risk register as its risk rating. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Use the score as one input beside asset impact and exposure
options.B: Accept the proposal as a consistent industry-standard rating
options.C: Use each finding's environment-adjusted CVSS score as its rating
options.D: Rate each finding scored above 7.0 as a high register risk

questions.key_concept: A CVSS score is a severity input; a risk rating also needs the asset's business impact, its exposure and the likelihood of exploitation.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a CVSS score measures and what a register rating is used to decide.
questions.correct_explanation: A CVSS score, even fully adjusted, measures the technical severity of a flaw, and the CVSS specification calls it an input to risk assessment. Risk also depends on what the asset supports, how reachable it is and the business impact of exploitation, so the risk practitioner uses the score as one input to the scenario rating. An environment-adjusted score is a better input, but still a severity score, not a business risk rating.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because CVSS is widely used and consistent. But a standard severity score still describes the flaw, not the business harm if the asset is exploited.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice, since environmental and threat metrics add context. But an adjusted score is still a severity score; the rating also needs the business impact of exploitation.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a threshold looks consistent. But a fixed cutoff ranks findings by severity alone, with no view of which business process each asset supports.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a standard severity score as business risk, and D sets register ratings by a severity cutoff with no view of what each asset supports.
Final two: A beats C because environmental and threat metrics refine severity, but business impact still has to be combined with the score to rate risk.
Exam cue: CVSS rates the flaw, not the risk. Expect the key to combine the score with asset value, exposure and business impact.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Risk scenario development and evaluation. Tabletop exercise participants
questions.question: A risk practitioner is planning a tabletop exercise on a ransomware scenario at a food distributor. Which of the following participants is MOST important to include?

options.A: Owners of the processes the attack would halt
options.B: Control owners responsible for backup and recovery
options.C: Internal auditors who will assess the exercise results
options.D: A hired negotiator experienced in ransom demands

questions.key_concept: A tabletop exercise tests a scenario and its responses with the people who make the business decisions, so the affected process owners must take part.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a tabletop exercise is meant to test before choosing who must attend.
questions.correct_explanation: A tabletop is a discussion-based walkthrough that tests roles, coordination and decisions against a scenario. The decisions that matter in ransomware, such as which deliveries to stop, what to tell customers and when to switch to manual work, belong to the owners of the affected processes, so their presence matters most. Backup control owners are the runner-up: they matter for recovery steps, but cannot make the business calls the exercise is testing.

wrong_explanations.B: Backup control owners add recovery detail; however, without the process owners, the exercise cannot test the business decisions a ransomware attack forces.
wrong_explanations.C: Internal audit gives independent assurance and may review the results later; as participants, auditors would not make the response decisions being tested.
wrong_explanations.D: A negotiator is a specialist the distributor might call during a real attack; the exercise first needs the people who own the business decisions.

tips: Eliminate: C brings the third line into management's exercise as a participant, and D adds a specialist before the people who own the decisions.
Final two: A beats B because the business decisions belong to process owners; control owners explain recovery steps but cannot make those calls.
Exam cue: tabletop exercises test decisions as much as technology. The people who own the business impact must be in the room.

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Business impact analysis (BIA). Objective for the alternate site
questions.question: A risk practitioner is recording a bank's BIA results. Which objective is MOST appropriate for stating the share of normal branch payment volume that the alternate site must handle?

options.A: The recovery time objective
options.B: The recovery point objective
options.C: The acceptable interruption window
options.D: The service delivery objective

questions.key_concept: The service delivery objective sets the level of service needed during alternate processing; RTO and AIW are time limits, and RPO limits data loss.
questions.pre_read: Notice exactly what the objective must state.
questions.correct_explanation: The service delivery objective (SDO) is the level of service the business needs while it runs in alternate mode, until normal operation is restored. Stating the share of payment volume the alternate site must handle sets that level and drives the site's capacity. The RTO is the runner-up: it sets how soon payments must be running again, not how much service they must deliver once they are.

wrong_explanations.A: The RTO sets how soon payments must be running again after a disruption; however, it says nothing about how much volume the alternate site must then handle.
wrong_explanations.B: The RPO sets how much data loss is tolerable, which drives backup frequency; it does not set a level of service during alternate processing.
wrong_explanations.C: The AIW is the longest a system can be unavailable before objectives suffer; it is a time limit, not the service level required at the alternate site.

tips: Eliminate: B limits data loss, and C limits how long a system can be down; neither sets a service level.
Final two: D beats A because the bank must state how much service runs in alternate mode; the RTO only sets how soon recovery happens.
Exam cue: RTO, MTO and AIW say how soon; RPO says how much data; SDO says how much service while running in alternate mode.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Risk analysis methodologies. Equal scores on a matrix
questions.question: On a bank's risk matrix, card skimming (40 small losses a year) and a week-long banking outage (once in 20 years) both score 10. How should the risk analyst BEST present them to the committee?

options.A: With likelihood and impact shown for each scenario
options.B: As equal-priority scenarios with the same score
options.C: With the outage ranked higher for its larger impact
options.D: With each score converted to a loss figure in dollars

questions.key_concept: A combined matrix score shows order, not the shape of a risk; equal scores can hide very different likelihood and impact that need different responses.
questions.pre_read: Notice how each scenario reaches its score of 10.
questions.correct_explanation: The equal scores hide two different risks: about 40 small skimming losses a year call for mitigating controls, while a severe outage expected once in 20 years may call for continuity planning or transfer. Showing likelihood and impact separately lets the committee see that difference. Treating them as equal priorities is the runner-up: the matrix does rank them equally, but the score is ordinal and the decision needs the shape behind it.

wrong_explanations.B: The shared score is a fair ranking signal; however, it hides whether the risk comes from frequency or severity, which the committee needs to choose responses.
wrong_explanations.C: Ranking on impact alone drops likelihood, so the frequent skimming losses would be undervalued however often they occur.
wrong_explanations.D: Converting ordinal matrix scores into money produces precise-looking numbers the data does not support, adding false precision instead of clarity.

tips: Eliminate: C ranks on one dimension only, and D turns ordinal scores into invented money figures.
Final two: A beats B because equal scores can hide opposite risk profiles; showing both dimensions gives the committee what it needs to choose different responses.
Exam cue: matrix scores are ordinal. When the decision depends on how a risk arises, report likelihood and impact, not just the combined score.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Risk register. Ratings that judge a plan
questions.question: City council members ask whether the treatment plans in the IT risk register will bring each risk within appetite once completed. Which register field should the risk practitioner use to BEST answer them?

options.A: The target rating each planned response is set to reach
options.B: The current rating, with the controls in place today
options.C: The inherent rating, before controls are counted
options.D: The status of each action plan against its due date

questions.key_concept: Whether a treatment plan is enough is judged on its target risk, the Glossary's future residual risk, compared with appetite.
questions.pre_read: Notice the point in time the members are asking about.
questions.correct_explanation: The members want to know where each risk will land when its plan is done, which is the target, or future residual, risk the plan is designed to reach. Comparing that rating with appetite shows whether each plan is enough. The current rating is the runner-up: it is the right figure for today's position against appetite, but it cannot show where a plan will take the risk.

wrong_explanations.B: Current risk shows today's exposure and is compared with appetite now; it does not show where a completed plan would leave each risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Inherent risk ignores all controls and responses, so it cannot show the effect of any treatment plan.
wrong_explanations.D: Action status shows progress against dates, not the level of risk the finished plan will leave.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves out every response by definition, so it cannot show a plan's effect, and D tracks progress dates rather than any risk level.
Final two: A beats B because the question is about the plans once complete; current risk answers where the risk stands today.
Exam cue: today's position against appetite is current risk; whether a plan is enough is judged on its target, or future residual, risk.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Risk scenario development and evaluation. A bought scenario library
questions.question: A credit union's new risk function must build its first IT scenario set and has bought a library of 60 generic scenarios. What is the risk practitioner's BEST use of the library?

options.A: The full set, rated as the credit union bought it
options.B: A check run after scenarios are written from scratch
options.C: Evidence for regulators that coverage is complete
options.D: A starting list tailored to the credit union's processes

questions.key_concept: A generic scenario library is a starting point: tailor its scenarios to the enterprise's own processes, assets and objectives before rating them.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each use of the library gives the new set.
questions.correct_explanation: A library gives a quick, broad starting list, but its generic scenarios know nothing of the credit union's members, systems or controls. Tailoring each to the credit union's processes and assets, and dropping those that do not fit, gives scenarios owners can rate. Writing from scratch, then checking against the library, is the runner-up: it can catch gaps, but it redoes work the library holds, which is meant as a starting list to tailor.

wrong_explanations.A: Generic scenarios rated as written describe a typical firm, not this credit union, so their ratings would not reflect its own processes, assets or controls.
wrong_explanations.B: Drafting from scratch can catch gaps, but it redoes work the library already holds; generic scenarios are meant as a starting list each enterprise tailors.
wrong_explanations.C: A bought library shows what typical firms face, not that this credit union's own risks are covered; coverage comes from a set fitted to its processes.

tips: Eliminate: A rates generic scenarios as if they described this credit union, and C treats a generic library as proof its own risks are covered.
Final two: D beats B because tailoring the library gives breadth and fit in one pass; drafting from scratch first redoes work the library holds.
Exam cue: a generic scenario library is a starting list; tailor each scenario to the enterprise's own processes before rating it.

questions.subtopic: 2A2 Threat modeling and threat landscape. Threat model for a chatbot
questions.question: A savings bank plans a customer chatbot that answers from account data. The bank's threat model for the chatbot uses STRIDE alone. What should the risk practitioner recommend FIRST?

options.A: Rely on STRIDE's tampering and disclosure categories
options.B: Add an output filter before the chatbot goes live
options.C: Add AI attack classes such as prompt injection
options.D: Replace the threat model with a penetration test

questions.key_concept: Threat models for AI systems add AI attack classes, such as prompt injection, that general methods like STRIDE do not prompt.
questions.pre_read: Weigh each option by what it adds before go-live.
questions.correct_explanation: STRIDE prompts general threat types against a design, but it was not built around attacks on models, such as prompt injection that steers the chatbot into revealing account data. Adding AI attack classes, as NIST AI 100-2 catalogs them, completes the model before controls are chosen. An output filter is the runner-up: it may become a control, but choosing it before the AI threats are modeled guesses at which attacks it must stop.

wrong_explanations.A: STRIDE's categories are broad, but they do not prompt AI-specific attacks such as prompt injection, so threats unique to the chatbot could be missed.
wrong_explanations.B: An output filter may be a useful control, but choosing it before the AI threats are identified guesses at what it must block.
wrong_explanations.D: A penetration test checks a built system for exploitable weaknesses; it does not replace modeling threats during design, before controls are chosen.

tips: Eliminate: A trusts general categories to catch AI-specific attacks, and D swaps design-time modeling for a later test of the built system.
Final two: C beats B because the threats must be identified before a control is chosen; the filter may follow from the completed model.
Exam cue: a threat model for an AI system adds AI attack classes, such as prompt injection, to general methods like STRIDE.

questions.subtopic: 2A2 Threat modeling and threat landscape. Filtering threat alerts
questions.question: A dental clinic chain runs an online booking app and uses one brand of VPN for staff. Which of the following threat alerts should its risk analyst treat as MOST relevant?

options.A: A flaw in a VPN brand the chain does not use
options.B: A campaign against healthcare firms using its VPN brand
options.C: A worldwide rise in reported ransomware attacks
options.D: A nation-state campaign against defense contractors

questions.key_concept: Threat intelligence matters when it is relevant: an actor targeting the enterprise's sector and a technology it uses.
questions.pre_read: Check each alert against what the stem says about the chain.
questions.correct_explanation: Intelligence is filtered for relevance on two tests: does the actor target this kind of organization, and does the enterprise use the targeted technology? Only the campaign against healthcare firms using the chain's VPN brand passes both, so it is the alert to weigh in the scenarios first. The worldwide ransomware rise is the runner-up: it is real background, but it names neither the chain's sector nor its technology.

wrong_explanations.A: A flaw in a product the chain does not run cannot be exploited against it, however severe the flaw is.
wrong_explanations.C: A global trend is useful background, but it is not tied to the chain's sector or technology, so it adds little to its scenarios.
wrong_explanations.D: The campaign targets defense contractors, a sector the chain is not in, so the actor's intent does not extend to it.

tips: Eliminate: A concerns a product the chain does not use, and D targets a sector the chain is not in.
Final two: B beats C because it matches both the chain's sector and its technology; a global trend matches neither.
Exam cue: weigh threat intelligence by relevance: the enterprise's sector, its technology and its assets.

questions.subtopic: 2A2 Threat modeling and threat landscape. Fraud after multifactor sign-in
questions.question: A retailer added multifactor sign-in to its website. Takeovers there fell 80%, and the risk was re-rated within appetite. But account takeovers by impostors using call-center resets tripled. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Have the owner accept the re-rated takeover risk
options.B: Ask the call-center owner to add caller checks
options.C: Re-rate account takeover across both channels
options.D: Track the account resets until next quarter's review

questions.key_concept: Attackers blocked on one path shift to another, so rate a control's effect across every route to the same harm before relying on it.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the new rating covers with everything the stem says changed.
questions.correct_explanation: Attackers stopped on one path can move to an easier one; NIST SP 800-30 calls this threat shifting. The 80% fall measures only the website, while the call-center resets give the same attackers the same accounts, so the within-appetite rating covers part of the exposure. Re-rating across both channels comes first. Owner acceptance is the runner-up: the risk reads as within appetite, but on a rating that leaves out the path the attackers moved to.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting, as the risk was re-rated within appetite. But that rating counts only the website; accepting it would accept an exposure that now runs, unmeasured, through the call center.
wrong_explanations.B: Caller checks may follow, but asking the call-center owner for them now fixes a single path before anyone knows the shifted risk's size or the risk owner has decided.
wrong_explanations.D: The rise came alongside the new control and hands over the same accounts; waiting a quarter leaves a within-appetite rating resting on half the picture.

tips: Eliminate: B picks a fix before the shifted risk is rated, and D waits a quarter while impostors take accounts by phone.
Final two: C beats A because the within-appetite rating covers only the website; acceptance needs a rating of every path, and this one misses the channel the attackers moved to.
Exam cue: when a control cuts attacks on one path, look for the attackers on another; re-rate every route to the same harm before relying on the result.

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Business impact analysis (BIA). Recovery rank cited for a data leak
questions.question: A retailer's AI model is trained on customer purchase histories. The BIA ranks this data low for recovery. So the model owner rates the impact of a leak or tampering as low. What is the risk analyst's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The model owner, not IT, proposed the impact ratings
options.B: The BIA leaves out how likely an outage of the data is
options.C: The recovery rank reflects only the harm of an outage
options.D: The BIA rank that the owner cited ignored IT's restore times

questions.key_concept: A BIA recovery rank measures the harm of losing access to a resource over time, not the harm of its data leaking or being altered.
questions.pre_read: Note what the BIA measured and what the owner is now rating.
questions.correct_explanation: A BIA weighs criticality and sensitivity, but a recovery rank is its criticality result: it shows how fast harm grows while a resource is unavailable, so a low rank means the business can wait. It says nothing about purchase histories leaking or tampering that poisons the next model, so those scenarios need their own impact ratings. The BIA's silence on likelihood is the runner-up: true of every BIA, but these ratings are about impact.

wrong_explanations.A: Proposing impact is the business owner's role, since the business bears the harm; the flaw is the evidence the owner cited, not who cited it.
wrong_explanations.B: A BIA leaves out likelihood by design and still gives sound impact figures for outages; the problem is that a leak or tampering is not an outage.
wrong_explanations.D: Recovery priority comes from how long the business can wait, which the owner judges, not from IT's restore times, which would say nothing about a leak or tampering either.

tips: Eliminate: A objects to the business owner proposing impact, which is the owner's role, and D wants IT's restore times in a priority the business decides.
Final two: C beats B because the ratings concern impact; the BIA's impact figures measure outage harm, not the harm of a leak or of tampering.
Exam cue: a BIA recovery rank answers how long the business can wait for a resource; rate leak and tampering scenarios on their own harm.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Risk analysis methodologies. Yearly reserve sized to the ALE
questions.question: A paint maker's ransomware scenario for its warehouse has a $1,000,000 SLE and a 5% ARO. The risk owner plans a $50,000 yearly reserve to cover it. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Find out what cyber insurance cover for the scenario would cost
options.B: Have the risk owner re-rate the scenario low from its ALE
options.C: Credit the risk owner's reserve as a control in the rating
options.D: Show the risk owner that one event costs 20 times the reserve

questions.key_concept: ALE spreads a rare loss across years; for rare, severe events, the owner also needs the single loss before choosing a response.
questions.pre_read: Work out the ALE, then compare it with what one event would cost.
questions.correct_explanation: The ALE is $1,000,000 × 0.05 = $50,000, so the reserve matches the expected yearly loss, yet one event costs $1,000,000, 20 times a year's reserve, and could strike in the first year. The owner needs that single-loss figure before deciding how to fund or treat the risk. Pricing cyber insurance is the runner-up: a reasonable option to explore, but it picks a response before the owner understands the exposure.

wrong_explanations.A: Insurance may suit, but pricing it chooses a response before the owner sees that the plan rests on a misread ALE; the decision basis comes first.
wrong_explanations.B: A small ALE does not mean low risk: a $1,000,000 event expected once in 20 years can exceed what the firm can absorb in the year it happens.
wrong_explanations.C: A reserve pays for losses after an event; it lowers neither likelihood nor impact, so crediting it as a control would understate current risk.

tips: Eliminate: B reads a small ALE as low risk, and C credits a funding reserve as a control, though it lowers neither likelihood nor impact.
Final two: D beats A because the owner's plan reads the ALE as the yearly cash need; show the single loss first, then weigh options such as insurance.
Exam cue: for rare, severe events, report the single loss beside the ALE; a yearly average can mask a loss the enterprise cannot absorb at once.

questions.subtopic: 2B1 Risk assessment concepts and standards. Controllers moved to a hotter site
questions.question: A textile mill's loom controllers, with two faults in eight years, were moved last month beside new dryers and now run 15°C hotter. Which is the BEST basis for the risk analyst's fault-likelihood rating?

options.A: Threat reports on attacks against textile control systems
options.B: The mill's own eight-year fault record for the controllers
options.C: The line owner's estimate of the controllers' remaining life
options.D: The maker's failure-rate data at the new operating temperature

questions.key_concept: Own history predicts equipment failure best while conditions hold; after a change such as more heat, prefer data for the new conditions.
questions.pre_read: Ask under what conditions each source's figures were gathered.
questions.correct_explanation: A controller fault is a non-adversarial event, rated from historical and empirical data, and running hotter changes how often electronics fail. The maker's failure-rate data at the new temperature describes the controllers as they now run. The mill's own eight-year record is the runner-up: own history is usually the best source, but it was gathered in cooler conditions that no longer apply.

wrong_explanations.A: Threat reports describe attackers, but a controller fault is a non-adversarial event; its likelihood comes from failure data, not intent or capability.
wrong_explanations.B: Own history is normally the best basis, but these eight years were spent in cooler conditions, so they may understate faults at the new, hotter site.
wrong_explanations.C: An estimate of remaining life is one person's judgment, a fallback when data is missing; measured failure rates are stronger evidence.

tips: Eliminate: A treats an equipment fault as an attack, and C relies on one person's judgment where measured failure data exists.
Final two: D beats B because the eight-year record was gathered in cooler conditions; the maker's data matches how the controllers now run.
Exam cue: past records predict best while conditions hold; after a move, an upgrade or a new load, look for data that fits the new conditions.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Risk register. Showing supplier risks together
questions.question: An e-scooter rental operator's board wants its supplier-related risks shown together, but each of the 140 register entries records only a scenario, owner and ratings. Which change should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: A list of supplier entries compiled by each risk owner
options.B: A keyword search of scenarios that name a supplier
options.C: A risk category on each entry, chosen from one agreed list
options.D: A separate register for supplier risks with procurement as owner

questions.key_concept: A risk category on every register entry, drawn from one agreed list, lets entries be grouped, compared and combined, such as all supplier risks.
questions.pre_read: Weigh how each option would find every relevant entry, and keep finding them.
questions.correct_explanation: A category field drawn from one agreed list lets the register be filtered and combined by theme, so supplier risks can be shown together now and each time the profile is reported, and the same entries can roll up to the enterprise view. A keyword search is the runner-up: it is quick, but it misses scenarios that do not name a supplier and depends on who picks the search words.

wrong_explanations.A: Owners' lists answer this request once, in each owner's own terms; nothing in the register then lets the next request be met the same way.
wrong_explanations.B: A search finds only scenarios that happen to name a supplier and depends on who picks the words, so results are incomplete and hard to repeat.
wrong_explanations.D: A separate register splits the risk profile, so supplier risks can no longer be compared or combined with the rest; one register with categories avoids that.

tips: Eliminate: A is a one-off list in each owner's own terms, and D splits supplier risks from the rest of the profile, so they cannot be combined.
Final two: C beats B because an agreed category finds every supplier entry the same way each time; a keyword search misses entries that name no supplier.
Exam cue: to group, compare or roll up register entries, look for a common field, such as a category, drawn from one agreed list.

questions.subtopic: 2A1 Risk events. CVs sent without consent
questions.question: A recruitment firm records each CV it sends and each candidate's consent in its CRM. Which source would BEST show the risk analyst how often consultants send CVs without consent?

options.A: Complaint records in the CRM about CVs sent without consent
options.B: CRM records of CVs sent without any matching consent entry
options.C: Regulator notices fining other recruiters for the practice
options.D: The placements process owner's estimate of its frequency

questions.key_concept: Complaints capture only events people notice and report; a complete record of every transaction shows far more reliably how often an event occurs.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each source would miss.
questions.correct_explanation: Every CV sent and every consent is recorded in the CRM, so matching the two finds each unconsented submission, whether or not anyone noticed it. That complete count is the firm's own event record for the scenario. Complaints are the runner-up: they are a real internal source, but they count only the cases a candidate noticed and chose to report, so they understate how often it happens.

wrong_explanations.A: Complaints are a real internal source, but they count only the submissions a candidate learned of and chose to report, so they understate how often it happens.
wrong_explanations.C: Enforcement against other recruiters shows the consequence and that the practice exists in the sector, not how often this firm's consultants do it.
wrong_explanations.D: An owner's estimate is judgment, useful when records are missing; here the CRM holds every submission and consent, which is stronger evidence.

tips: Eliminate: C describes other firms' penalties rather than this firm's frequency, and D offers one person's judgment where complete records exist.
Final two: B beats A because matching every submission to its consent finds each event, while complaints catch only those a candidate noticed and reported.
Exam cue: for how often an event occurs, prefer a complete internal record of every transaction over sources that depend on someone noticing and speaking up.

questions.subtopic: 2B1 Risk assessment concepts and standards. Yearly radar network assessment
questions.question: A weather service's risk team redoes its full radar network assessment yearly. Since the last one, monitoring shows only a new threat group and two retired radars. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the team assess just the risk factors that changed
options.B: Repeat the full assessment from scratch with the radar owners
options.C: Carry the previous ratings forward without the two radars
options.D: Swap the assessment for each radar owner's self-rating

questions.key_concept: Maintaining an assessment means monitoring its risk factors and, unless a significant change calls for a full redo, assessing the factors that changed.
questions.pre_read: Note what the stem says monitoring already shows before deciding how much to redo.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST SP 800-30 treats maintenance as monitoring risk factors and updating the assessment with the results. Unless a significant change calls for revisiting the whole assessment, an update assesses just the factors that changed: here the new threat group and the retired radars. Repeating the full assessment with the radar owners is the runner-up: it is thorough and involves the owners, but it re-rates what monitoring shows is unchanged.

wrong_explanations.B: A full redo is thorough and involves the owners, but without a significant change it spends the effort re-rating factors that monitoring shows have not changed.
wrong_explanations.C: Dropping the retired radars is right, but carrying the rest forward ignores the new threat group, a changed risk factor the update has to assess.
wrong_explanations.D: Owners' self-ratings replace analysis with judgment and lose the assessment's common method, so the ratings cannot be compared with each other or with appetite.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves out the new threat group that monitoring found, and D replaces the assessment's common method with each owner's own judgment.
Final two: A beats B because, with no significant change, an update assesses the factors that changed; a full redo spends its effort re-rating what monitoring shows is stable.
Exam cue: an assessment stays live through monitoring; redo it in full after a significant change, and otherwise update the factors that have moved.

questions.subtopic: 2B5 Inherent and residual risk. Backup credit in a ransomware rating
questions.question: A pest-control firm rates residual risk for ransomware encrypting its scheduling system. The rating cuts both likelihood and impact because of offline backups that pass full-restore tests. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Re-rate impact on how long a complete restore of the system takes
options.B: Re-rate likelihood with the risk owner, without backup credit
options.C: Credit the backups in the inherent rating too
options.D: Remove both cuts until a real attack proves the backups

questions.key_concept: A control earns credit on the factor it changes: offline backups shorten an outage and cut impact, but do not make an attack less likely.
questions.pre_read: Picture the attack happening, then ask what each control changes about it.
questions.correct_explanation: A control is credited on the factor it changes. Restore-tested offline backups shorten the outage, so they earn the impact cut, but they do nothing to stop ransomware encrypting the system, so the likelihood cut has no control behind it. Re-rating impact on restore time is the runner-up: tying impact credit to recovery time is sound, but the error in this rating is the unsupported likelihood cut.

wrong_explanations.A: Tying impact credit to restore time is sound practice, but the tested backups already support the impact cut; the rating's error is the likelihood cut no control supports.
wrong_explanations.C: Inherent risk credits no control, so adding the backups there would hide how much the scenario depends on them working.
wrong_explanations.D: Restore tests are evidence that the backups work, so the impact cut is earned now; waiting for a real attack withholds credit the tests support.

tips: Eliminate: C puts a control into inherent risk, which credits none, and D withholds impact credit that passed restore tests already support.
Final two: B beats A because backups act on impact, not on whether ransomware strikes; refining the impact cut leaves the unsupported likelihood cut in place.
Exam cue: credit each control on the factor it changes; backups and other recovery controls lower impact, so a likelihood cut needs a control that stops the event.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Vulnerability management. Online shop on a SaaS platform
questions.question: A cider maker's online shop runs on a SaaS platform. The IT manager wants the shop left out of vulnerability identification, since the provider patches the platform. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Take the provider's patching record as the shop's risk rating
options.B: Obtain the provider's latest independent assurance report
options.C: Ask IT to check the shop settings the firm itself controls
options.D: Scan the provider's servers with the IT team's own scanner

questions.key_concept: In a SaaS service the provider patches the platform, but the customer's own settings, accounts and integrations stay within its vulnerability identification.
questions.pre_read: Before agreeing to leave a rented service out, work out who controls each part of it.
questions.correct_explanation: In a SaaS service the provider patches the platform, but the customer still controls its own settings: admin accounts, staff access, add-ons and payment links. Weaknesses there are the cider maker's to find, and its IT team, which runs its technical controls, is the one to check them. The provider's assurance report is the runner-up: it covers the provider's controls, not how the cider maker has set up its own shop.

wrong_explanations.A: Patching covers flaws in the provider's software, the IT manager's premise; it says nothing about the shop's own accounts and settings, so it cannot stand as the shop's rating.
wrong_explanations.B: An assurance report tests the provider's side of the service; weak admin accounts or risky add-ons the cider maker set up itself fall outside what it covers.
wrong_explanations.D: The servers belong to the provider, so scanning them needs its consent and tests its side of the service; the shop's own settings would still go unchecked.

tips: Eliminate: A accepts the premise that patching covers the whole shop, and D scans servers the firm does not own, which needs the provider's consent, and still misses the shop's settings.
Final two: C beats B because the firm still sets up its own shop's accounts, add-ons and settings; the provider's assurance report covers the provider's side, not the customer's setup.
Exam cue: for a cloud service, split the work by who controls what: the provider's assurance covers its part, and the customer checks the settings, accounts and integrations it controls.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Risk register. AI feature added by a vendor update
questions.question: A real estate agency's CRM is already in its register. A vendor update switched on an AI feature sending buyers' emails to an outside model to draft replies. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Get the CRM's owner to log the update as a routine change
options.B: Open a linked entry for the AI feature under a business owner
options.C: Widen the CRM's existing entry to cover the AI feature's risks
options.D: Use the vendor's own AI risk rating for the feature

questions.key_concept: An AI feature that adds a new data use and new harms gets its own register entry and owner, linked to the tool's entry.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the change alters a risk already recorded or brings a new one.
questions.correct_explanation: The feature brings a new data use, buyers' emails sent to an outside model, and new harms, such as invented claims in replies, that the CRM's entry never rated. Its own entry, with a business owner, gets that risk rated against appetite, and the link to the CRM's entry shows the dependency between them. Widening the CRM's entry is the runner-up: it blends two different risks into one rating and owner, hiding the new one.

wrong_explanations.A: An update that adds a new data use is not business as usual; logged as a routine change, the feature's risk is never rated or entered in the register.
wrong_explanations.C: One entry would blend the CRM's existing risk with a new data use and new harms, so neither rating shows clearly against appetite or reaches the right owner.
wrong_explanations.D: A vendor rates its feature for typical use; the agency's own data, buyers and appetite set the risk of this use, so the agency rates its own.

tips: Eliminate: A logs a new data use as a routine change, so its risk is never rated, and D takes the vendor's rating in place of the agency's own analysis.
Final two: B beats C because the feature adds a data use and harms the CRM's entry never rated; its own linked entry keeps both risks visible, each with the right owner.
Exam cue: when an existing tool gains an AI feature that adds a data use or new harms, give it its own register entry and owner, linked to the tool's entry, not folded in.

questions.subtopic: 2B5 Inherent and residual risk. Loss history used as inherent likelihood
questions.question: A claims adjusting firm set its payment-fraud scenario's inherent likelihood from five years of losses, all under today's payment controls. It then cut residual likelihood for those controls. What should concern the risk analyst MOST?

options.A: The loss history already carries the effect of those controls
options.B: Five years of losses are too few to rate likelihood
options.C: Inherent likelihood should also credit the payment controls
options.D: Records of fraud losses measure impact rather than likelihood

questions.key_concept: Loss history gathered under today's controls already reflects them; using it as inherent likelihood and then crediting the same controls counts them twice.
questions.pre_read: Note the conditions under which each input to the rating was gathered.
questions.correct_explanation: Losses incurred under today's payment controls show how often fraud gets past those controls, which is close to current likelihood, not inherent. Cutting residual likelihood again for the same controls credits them twice and understates the risk. Too short a history is the runner-up: more years would firm up the figure, but any history taken under these controls would still include their effect.

wrong_explanations.B: A longer history would firm up the estimate, but it would still be history taken under the same controls, so the double credit would remain.
wrong_explanations.C: Inherent risk credits no control by definition; the problem is that the loss history already credits these controls without anyone saying so.
wrong_explanations.D: How often losses occur is a likelihood input and their amounts an impact input; loss records inform both.

tips: Eliminate: C would credit controls in inherent risk, which by definition credits none, and D treats loss records as impact data, though how often losses occur gives likelihood.
Final two: A beats B because every loss happened under today's controls; more years of the same history would still carry their effect, so crediting the controls again counts them twice.
Exam cue: history gathered under current controls shows current risk, not inherent risk; credit each control once, not again on top of data that already reflects it.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (inherent risk); ISACA Glossary (current risk); NIST IR 8286 Rev. 1 Section 3 (Cybersecurity Risk Considerations Throughout the ERM Process: registers typically record current risk, risk at least partially addressed by management actions)

questions.subtopic: 2A1 Risk events. Large forged payment stopped at a pickle maker
questions.question: A pickle maker's payment-fraud scenario assumes ten attempts a year and losses up to $20,000. A clerk has stopped a forged $250,000 supplier payment. What does this near miss MOST show the risk analyst?

options.A: Payment checks strong enough to justify a lower rating
options.B: Impact rated too low for frauds of this size
options.C: Likelihood rated too low for the attempts seen
options.D: A loss event to log at the full $250,000

questions.key_concept: A near miss shows size as well as frequency; an attempt far above a scenario's rated loss shows its impact is rated too low.
questions.pre_read: Hold the near miss against each half of the rating: how often attempts were expected, and how large a loss was assumed.
questions.correct_explanation: The scenario already expects about ten attempts a year, so one more attempt fits its likelihood. Its size does not fit: had the forged payment gone through, the loss would have been $250,000, over twelve times the $20,000 the rating allows. That is impact evidence for the risk owner to weigh. Likelihood rated too low is the runner-up: near misses can be likelihood evidence, but this attempt sits within the expected rate.

wrong_explanations.A: One stopped attempt does not show the checks will stop the next large one, and it revealed a loss far above the rating; it gives no basis for lowering it.
wrong_explanations.C: Near misses can be likelihood evidence, but the scenario already assumes about ten attempts a year; one more fits that rate, while its size does not fit the impact.
wrong_explanations.D: No money left the firm, so this is a near miss, not a loss event; the $250,000 is the loss it would have caused, which informs the impact rating.

tips: Eliminate: A lowers a rating on one stopped attempt that revealed a bigger loss, and D logs a loss event although no money left the firm.
Final two: B beats C because the scenario already expects about ten attempts a year; this attempt fits that rate, but its $250,000 size is over twelve times the rated loss.
Exam cue: read a near miss against both halves of the rating; an attempt that fits the expected frequency but far exceeds the rated loss is impact evidence.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Risk scenario development and evaluation. Map model that learns from drivers' reports
questions.question: A map data provider's model learns from drivers' reports. The model's draft scenario covers delays from honest errors. Groups flooded rival apps with fake closures. Which of the following should the risk analyst add FIRST?

options.A: The data science lead as the scenario's co-owner
options.B: A screening check on reports before each retraining
options.C: Coordinated false reports as a threat source and event
options.D: The model's gradual drift as roads change

questions.key_concept: A model learning from user reports can be poisoned by coordinated false input; its scenario names that threat source and event before controls are chosen.
questions.pre_read: List the scenario elements the draft already has, then compare them with what the stem says has happened elsewhere.
questions.correct_explanation: The model learns from what drivers send, so groups that flood it with false closures can poison it, as they did at rival apps. The draft names honest errors as the cause, so it cannot rate a coordinated attack with its likelihood and scale. Adding the groups as threat source and their false reports as event comes first. Screening reports before retraining is the runner-up: a likely control, chosen once the poisoning scenario is rated.

wrong_explanations.A: AI risk sits with a business owner, such as the head of the routing product; the data science lead may own controls, and co-owners blur who decides.
wrong_explanations.B: Screening may well be the right control, but it is chosen after the poisoning scenario is described and rated; it does not complete the scenario.
wrong_explanations.D: Drift is a real AI risk, but it has its own cause and scenario; it does not cover groups feeding the model false reports on purpose.

tips: Eliminate: A gives an AI risk to the data science lead as co-owner instead of a business owner, and D adds drift, a separate risk with a different cause.
Final two: C beats B because the draft has no deliberate attacker yet; the poisoning threat is added and rated before a screening control is chosen for it.
Exam cue: when a model learns from user input, a scenario of honest errors misses poisoning; add the coordinated threat source and event before choosing controls.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Vulnerability management. Reach of vulnerability identification at a solar panel maker
questions.question: Which of the following does a solar panel maker's risk analyst need FIRST for vulnerability identification to reach all of the firm's systems?

options.A: Rate of critical flaws patched within the target time
options.B: Vendor advisories giving CVSS scores for their products
options.C: Vendor reports on groups that target solar panel makers
options.D: A current inventory of hardware and software in use

questions.key_concept: Vulnerability identification reaches only the assets the firm knows it has, so a current hardware and software inventory comes first.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each option depends on before it can show a weakness in one of the firm's systems.
questions.correct_explanation: Vulnerability identification covers only what the firm knows it has: scans, advisories and reviews are matched against a current list of hardware and software, and anything missing from it goes unchecked. CSF 2.0 places these inventories under Asset Management, beside identifying vulnerabilities in assets. Vendor advisories are the runner-up: they report flaws in products, but without the inventory the analyst cannot tell which advisories apply to the firm.

wrong_explanations.A: A patching rate measures how fast known flaws are fixed; it says nothing about weaknesses in systems no one has listed.
wrong_explanations.B: Advisories describe flaws in vendors' products; until the analyst knows which products the firm runs, they cannot tell which advisories apply.
wrong_explanations.C: Reports on attacker groups describe threats, not weaknesses; they help rate likelihood but do not show which systems have flaws.

tips: Eliminate: A measures how fast known flaws are fixed, not where weaknesses are, and C describes threats, not vulnerabilities.
Final two: D beats B because advisories matter only once the analyst knows which products the firm runs; the inventory comes first, and advisories are matched against it.
Exam cue: vulnerability identification starts from knowing what you have; a current hardware and software inventory sets its reach, and unlisted systems go unchecked.
